title: What you will be able to do
instruction: Press reveal to see each outcome for this lesson.

_items.text: Form and justify a judgement on the relative importance of competing factors.

title: A judgement needs a reason
body: Saying one factor matters more than another is easy. Saying why, in a way someone else could check, is the actual skill this lesson is building.

title: The book's own formula
body: Dennis and Abbott (2026, pp.127-128) give the shape a justified judgement takes, set out as its own formula: 'X is more important (or significant or valuable) than Y because ....' Notice that the formula does not work without the 'because'.

title: Worked example
body:
Consider two drafts reaching the same conclusion about the same two factors.

{{learner-a}} writes that cost matters more than quality, and moves on without saying why.

{{learner-b}} writes that cost matters more than quality in this case, because the client's stated budget rules out every option that would improve quality.

Both drafts favoured cost over quality. Only {{learner-b}}'s judgement could actually be checked.

title: Why stating a criterion first helps
body: Naming your criterion, such as strength of evidence, size of effect, or fit with a stated constraint, before you rank anything means your judgement can be examined and challenged on that criterion, rather than taken on trust.

title: Criteria-stating checklist
body: Use these questions before you commit to a judgement about which factor matters most.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Did I name my criterion before ranking the factors?
Did I complete the 'because' in my own judgement?
Did I say what evidence would change my ranking?
Did I check my criterion against at least one alternative criterion?

displayTitle: Forming a judgement, move by move
instruction: Open each move to read it. You can keep more than one open at once.

_items.title: Move 1: Name the factors
_items.body: List the factors actually competing for importance, not just the one you already favour.
_items.advice: In practice: write every factor down before ranking any of them, even the ones you expect to dismiss.

_items.title: Move 2: State your criterion
_items.body: Decide what 'important' means here: strength of evidence, size of effect, or fit with a constraint.
_items.advice: In practice: name the criterion in one sentence before you rank anything against it.

_items.title: Move 3: Rank and justify
_items.body: Complete the formula: X is more important than Y because ....
_items.advice: In practice: if you cannot finish the sentence, your judgement is not ready yet.

_items.title: Move 4: Say what would change it
_items.body: State the evidence that would move your ranking, even if you do not expect to find it.
_items.advice: In practice: this is what separates a justified judgement from a fixed opinion.

title: Applying this to your own writing
body: Next time you rank factors in an assignment, write the criterion down first, then complete the formula properly. A judgement with its 'because' attached is one a marker, or a reader, can actually engage with.

title: Your turn
instruction: This is for your own reflection; no right answers are expected.

_items.text: Think of a judgement you have made recently, academic or otherwise. What was your criterion, even if you did not state it at the time?
What evidence would have to appear to change that judgement?
